issues.legal_issue: A statutory right of pre-emption based solely on ownership of adjoining property is an unreasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property when the law applies broadly to different kinds of property.
material_facts: The challenged law granted pre-emption to owners of adjoining property, including where the purchaser and pre-emptor both owned adjoining property.
The law applied to urban and rural property, including agricultural land and houses.
Even after notice of the proposed sale, a pre-emptor could bring a later suit by alleging that the stated price was not fixed in good faith, exposing the vendor and purchaser to litigation.
issues.conclusion: By a majority, the Court held the vicinage-based pre-emption provision invalid as an unreasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property; the appeal concerning that provision succeeded. The dissenting judges would have upheld it.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) guaranteed the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, subject under Article 19(5) to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The majority held that a customary right's earlier acceptance did not determine its reasonableness under the Constitution, and that a broad vicinage rule offered no sufficient general-public advantage to justify its burdens. The majority considered the reasoning in Shri Audh Behari Singh v. Gajadhar Jaipuria, Ibrahim Saib v. Muni Mir Udin Saib, and Mohomed Beg Amin v. Narayan Meghaji Patil; it held that even a right attaching to property could restrict the constitutional right. It also reasoned that excluding strangers from localities could not be justified by the former aim of preserving groups divided by religion, race, or caste, in light of Article 15.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_pre: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a right of pre-emption over property.
predicates.preemption_based_only_on_adjoining_owner: The law granted the pre-emption right because a claimant owned property adjoining the property being sold.
predicates.law_covers_urban_and_rural_property: The law applied across both urban and rural property, including property beyond agricultural holdings.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a property pre-emption law based only on adjoining ownership and the law applies broadly to urban and rural property, the rule treats that vicinage-based right as an unreasonable property restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A preference among otherwise eligible pre-emptors based on their relationship to the seller does not itself invalidate a co-ownership-based pre-emption right when it merely ranks competing claimants.
material_facts: The challenged law ranked persons in the same class of pre-emptors by preferring the person nearer in relationship to the seller.
The law also granted a pre-emption right to co-sharers, a ground the Court did not find invalid.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the relationship-based preference survived for the co-sharer ground, although the vicinage ground was invalidated. The dissenting judges considered the preference valid as part of the overall right.
issues.legal_principle: The majority treated the preference as a mechanism for resolving competition among persons who already had a valid right, rather than as an independent source of pre-emption. It therefore survived to the extent it operated with the valid co-sharer ground.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preemption_p: A party challenged a rule that ranks persons entitled to pre-empt a sale.
predicates.multiple_claimants_have_a_valid_coowners: More than one claimant is eligible for pre-emption on the basis of co-ownership, which is otherwise a valid ground.
predicates.kinship_only_ranks_those_claimants: The preference based on relationship determines which eligible claimant has priority without independently creating the underlying pre-emption right.

issues.definition: When a challenged priority rule ranks multiple claimants who already have a valid co-ownership-based pre-emption right solely by their relationship to the seller, the rule leaves that priority effective for the valid co-ownership right.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption right in favour of co-sharers in urban property is a reasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The challenged provision granted a pre-emption right to co-sharers in urban property.
The sale of a share to an outsider could introduce a stranger into shared ownership and make common management difficult.
The property at issue was a house, and the provision concerned urban property.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the co-sharer ground was valid and did not violate the constitutional property right.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 19(1)(f) and Article 19(5), holding that the benefit of preserving common ownership and facilitating management could outweigh the restrictions on the vendor and purchaser. It approved the treatment of co-sharer pre-emption in Uttam Singh v. Kartar Singh and Sardha Ram v. Haji Abdul Majid Mohd. Amir Khan.

predicates.preemption_favours_existing_coshareholde: The law gives persons who already share ownership priority to acquire the interest being sold.
predicates.sale_would_introduce_an_outsider_into_sh: Without the pre-emption right, a purchaser outside the existing group of co-owners could become a co-owner.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a law that gives existing co-sharers priority and a sale could introduce an outsider into shared ownership, the rule treats the co-sharer right as a reasonable property restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption right in favour of owners whose properties share a staircase with the property being sold is a reasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The challenged provision granted pre-emption to owners of other properties sharing a staircase with the property being sold.
The Court considered that sale to a stranger could give that stranger a right to use the common staircase and cause serious inconvenience to the other owners.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the common-staircase ground was valid and did not violate the constitutional property right.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Article 19(1)(f) and Article 19(5), the Court treated the shared-staircase ground as practically analogous to co-sharer pre-emption because it protects the owners' shared use of property and avoids the disadvantages of introducing an outsider. The Court applied its reasoning on co-sharer rights, including that reflected in Uttam Singh v. Kartar Singh and Sardha Ram v. Haji Abdul Majid Mohd. Amir Khan.

predicates.sale_would_give_an_outsider_shared_stair: Without the pre-emption right, the purchaser would acquire a property carrying a right to use a staircase shared with other owners.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a law that gives priority to owners sharing a staircase and a sale would give an outsider shared use of it, the rule treats the pre-emption right as a reasonable property restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption right in favour of owners of properties sharing a common entrance from the street with the property being sold is a reasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The challenged provision granted pre-emption to owners of other properties sharing a common entrance from the street with the property being sold.
The Court considered that the shared entrance placed the owners in a position similar to co-sharers and that sale to a stranger could disrupt their shared arrangement.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the common-entrance ground was valid and did not violate the constitutional property right.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 19(1)(f) and Article 19(5). It held that owners sharing a private entrance from a public street were sufficiently similar to co-sharers for the same public-interest reasoning to apply. The Court applied its reasoning on co-sharer rights, including that reflected in Uttam Singh v. Kartar Singh and Sardha Ram v. Haji Abdul Majid Mohd. Amir Khan.

predicates.sale_would_introduce_an_outsider_to_the_: Without the pre-emption right, the purchaser would become an owner using an entrance shared with the other properties.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a law that gives priority to owners sharing an entrance and a sale would introduce an outsider to that shared entrance, the rule treats the pre-emption right as a reasonable property restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory pre-emption right based on ownership of property contiguous to the property being sold is an unreasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The challenged provision granted pre-emption to persons owning property contiguous to the property being sold.
The law applied to urban immovable property, and the claimed right was based on vicinage rather than co-ownership or a shared facility.
issues.conclusion: By a majority, the Court held the contiguous-property ground invalid for the same reasons that made the other vicinage-based pre-emption provision invalid. The dissenting judges would have upheld it.
issues.legal_principle: The majority applied Article 19(1)(f) and Article 19(5), holding that pre-emption based on vicinage was not a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public. Its reasoning in the related vicinage challenge included that a prior custom did not conclusively establish constitutional reasonableness and that excluding strangers from an area could not be justified by divisions based on religion, race, or caste, given Article 15. The majority also considered Shri Audh Behari Singh v. Gajadhar Jaipuria, Ibrahim Saib v. Muni Mir Udin Saib, and Mohomed Beg Amin v. Narayan Meghaji Patil.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_pre: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a right of pre-emption over property.
predicates.preemption_based_only_on_contiguous_owne: The law grants the pre-emption right because the claimant owns property contiguous to the property being sold, without requiring co-ownership or a shared facility.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a pre-emption right based only on contiguous ownership, the rule treats that right as an unreasonable property restriction.

issues.legal_issue: Exempting agricultural property and certain commercial or public-use premises from an urban-property pre-emption law does not make the law discriminatory when those properties form distinct classes from private residential property.
material_facts: The challenged law applied to urban immovable property but excluded agricultural property and premises such as shops, inns, market enclosures, places of worship, and similar buildings.
The Court treated agricultural property as a distinct class and treated the other exempted premises as places to which the public resorted, distinct from private residential property.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the challenged provision did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality on account of those exclusions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 and held that the excluded properties could be treated as distinct classes from private residential property. It referred to Karim Ahmad v. Rahmat Elahi in discussing the meaning of a market enclosure.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge_to_pro: A party alleged that a property pre-emption law discriminated between classes of property owners or properties.
predicates.law_distinguishes_private_residences_fro: The law excludes agricultural property or premises to which the public resorts while applying to private residential property.
predicates.those_property_types_are_distinct_classe: The excluded agricultural or public-use premises differ in relevant character from private residential property.

issues.definition: When an equality challenge concerns a law distinguishing private residences from agricultural or public-resort property, and those types are distinct classes, the rule treats the classification as non-discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption right among occupants of agricultural land within a survey unit is a reasonable restriction when the occupants are co-sharers or akin to co-sharers and the right promotes consolidation of holdings.
material_facts: The right applied to unalienated land held for agricultural purposes and was limited to occupants holding interests within the same survey number.
The holders of a survey number were jointly responsible for the land revenue, and holders of subdivisions within it were akin to co-sharers.
The right applied to specified transfers to strangers and did not arise for an exchange of land with an occupant of another survey number.
Exercising the right could consolidate agricultural holdings within the survey number.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the pre-emption provisions as constitutional and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 19(1)(f), subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public under Article 19(5), the Court held that a right confined to co-sharers or persons akin to co-sharers could protect common ownership and promote consolidation of agricultural holdings. It approved Ramchandra Krishnaji Dhagale v. Janardan Krishnappa Marwar.
